newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenyan officials say public share issues slow.
newsitem.headline: Kenyan officials say public share issues slow.

text.p: Kenyan bourse players said on Friday that new public share issues, seen as critical for faster growth of the Nairobi Stock Exchange, were not very encouraging.
But regulatory Capital Markets Authority (CMA) and Nairobi Stock Exchange (NSE) officials said they still hoped for at least 15 public companies seeking listing before the year 2000.

Kenyan privatisation officials said the process had reached complex companies -- such as Kenya Posts & Telecommunications and Kenya Railways -- which needed restructuring and a possible foreign partner before a final public offer.
The government lists these as strategic companies. Part of their problem includes restructuring huge debts, officials say.
"Public issues are not encouraging," said Paul Melly, chief executive at the Capital Markets Authority.
Kenya's finance ministry last month said in its quarterly budget report that privatisations were too slow.
In the only so-far announced initial public share offer, the government will sell 23.3 percent of its stake in the luxury Serena Lodges & Hotels chain from March 24 to April 14.
The stake, or 9,025,100 shares, will be sold at a price of 13 shillings (23 U.S. cents) per share.
Privatisation officials say Mumias Sugar Co, managed by a subsidiary of Tate & Lyle, will be floated some time this year.
"The most critical challenge facing the market is to increase supply of securities," said CMA's Melly said.

Nairobi Stock Exchange Chairman Jimnah Mbaru urged pension funds and insurance companies to seek listing to improve liquidity. Local insurance companies have complained that double taxation or discriminatory taxes keep them off the bourse.

Melly said CMA legislation would be reviewed to enhance its regulatory and development work and strengthen its independence. These measures would include creating an Appeals Tribunal to hear disputes of those not satisfied by its decisions.
"In addition, the Authority will establish operational rules and regulations on private placements of securities and collective investment vehicles," Melly added.
The Nairobi Stock Exchange has 60 listed companies and Melly sees these growing to 75 by the turn of the century.

Figures issued by the CMA showed that in 1991, the value of listed companies was 18 billion shillings but had grown to 107 billion shillings by end-1994, 106 billion at end-1995 and 100 billion at end-1996.
Volume of traded shares was posted at 16 million in 1991 and had reached 113 million shares in 1996. Turnover rose from 300 million in 1991 to 3.9 billion shillings in 1996.
Melly said: "If turnover has not reached 15 billion by the year 2000, I would consider that I have failed."
The figures showed that the share index rose from 961 in 1991 to a peak of 4,500 in 1994 and had dropped to 3,114. ($1=54.9 shillings).
